intro.title: Functional requirements
script: Before drawing anything I want to agree on **what Uber does** for this design. There are two kinds of user, **riders** and **drivers**, and the product is the moment they're brought together.

cards.title: Request a ride
lines: Upfront fare and ETA before confirming
script: A rider opens the app, sets a **pickup and dropoff**, and sees an **upfront fare and an ETA** before confirming.

cards.title: Driver availability
script: Meanwhile drivers who are **online** stream their GPS location continuously.

cards.title: Matching
lines: Never assign one driver to two trips
script: When a rider confirms, we **match** them with a nearby available driver. The invariant I care most about here: **one driver is never assigned to two trips**.

cards.title: Accept / decline
lines: Driver gets an offer with a ~15 s timeout
script: The driver gets an **offer** with a short timeout, around 15 seconds. If they decline or ignore it, we move on to the next driver.

cards.title: Live tracking
lines: and follows the trip on a map
script: Once matched, the rider watches the car **approach on a map**.

cards.title: Trip lifecycle
script: The trip moves through a **lifecycle**: requested, matched, arriving, in progress, completed, with cancellation possible at most steps.

cards.title: Dynamic pricing
script: Prices are **dynamic**: when demand outstrips supply in an area, a surge multiplier applies.

cards.title: Payment
lines: Charge the card on file, exactly once
script: At the end we **charge the card on file exactly once** and credit the driver.

cards.title: Ratings & history
lines: Riders and drivers rate each other
script: Both sides **rate** each other, and everyone can see their trip history and receipts.

outOfScope.title: Out of scope
script: I'm leaving out UberEats and delivery, Pool (shared rides change matching a lot), scheduled rides, in-app chat and calls, fraud and safety, and driver onboarding. I'm also **not designing the maps engine** itself. Routing over a road graph with live traffic is its own huge problem, so I'll treat "give me the route and ETA from A to B" as a service we call. The same goes for the internals of the card networks.
lines: UberEats & delivery  ·  Pool / shared rides  ·  Scheduled rides  ·  In-app chat & calls  ·  Fraud & safety  ·  Driver onboarding / KYC
Building the maps and routing engine (we call it as a service)  ·  Payment-processor internals

intro.title: Non-functional requirements
script: Now the qualities.

cards.title: Scale
script: For **scale** I'll assume about **20 million trips a day** worldwide and about **5 million drivers online** at the global peak.

cards.title: Match latency
script: Riders expect a **match within a few seconds**, which means the "who's near me" query needs to come back in well under 100 milliseconds.

cards.title: Fresh locations
lines: Lossy is OK, stale is not
script: Driver positions should be **at most a few seconds old**; dropping an update is fine, as the next one is coming anyway.

cards.title: Consistency
script: **Consistency is split down the middle**, and this shapes the whole design. Trip state and driver assignment must be **strongly consistent**: double-booking a driver or charging someone twice is a real failure. Locations and the map are **eventually consistent**: a car icon a second behind reality is fine.

cards.title: 99.99% available
script: The request path needs **four nines**, and a trip must survive the driver's phone going through a tunnel.

cards.title: Durability
script: Trips and payments are **durable**: once recorded, they are never lost. Location history is different; losing a few points of a driver's trail is harmless.

cards.title: Exactly-once pay
script: Payments are **exactly-once**.

cards.title: Geo-partitioned
lines: Demand is local: shard by city
script: Demand is intensely **local** (a rider in Paris never needs a driver in Tokyo), which is a gift for partitioning.

cards.title: Spiky
script: And traffic is **spiky**: a concert letting out puts 10× normal demand on a few city blocks.

estimates.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimates
script: The numbers. **Location writes**: 5 million drivers pinging every 4 seconds is about **1.25 million writes per second**. Compare that to **trips**: 20 million a day is only about 230 per second on average, maybe a couple of thousand at peak. The current location of every driver is about 5 million × 100 bytes, roughly **half a gigabyte**, so the whole live map fits in memory. Trip records are about 100 GB a day.
rows: fits in RAM, sharded by region

takeaway.title: Takeaway: a firehose and a trickle
script: So the takeaway: there are two very different problems here. A **firehose** of tiny, short-lived location writes that need fast spatial queries, and a **trickle** of trips that must be exact. I'll keep those two worlds separate throughout.
takeaway.heading: Takeaway: a firehose of locations and a trickle of trips that must be exact
lines: 1.25M location writes/s, each overwritten seconds later → an in-memory geo index, never a row in a SQL table
~1K trips/s with strict state and money attached → a small, strongly consistent store  ·  shard everything by city

slides.title: Start simple: two apps and one server
script: Let's start with the simplest system that could work. Two apps, **rider** and **driver**, and a **single server**.
The driver app, while online, sends the server its **GPS location every few seconds** over plain HTTPS. The server keeps a map of driver ID to latest position in memory.

slides.title: One ride, end to end, by polling
script: When a rider requests a ride, the server **scans every driver**, computes the straight-line distance to the pickup, and picks the closest one who isn't busy. The driver app is polling too, so on its next poll it sees "you have a ride request", and the driver taps accept. The rider app polls for status and the driver's position, and draws the car on a map.

steps.label: scan every driver: nearest free one

slides.title: The core loop
script: This actually works for a single small city. It nails down the **core loop** I want to keep in mind for the rest of the design: drivers report where they are, a rider asks for a ride, we pick a driver, the driver agrees, and both sides watch the trip progress.
But almost everything about it breaks at scale.

slides.title: What breaks first
script: Everything lives in one process's memory, so a restart loses every in-flight trip. The full scan is O(drivers) per request. Polling wastes battery and adds seconds of latency to every offer. And one box can't take a million writes a second. Let's fix these one at a time, starting with the most basic: durability.

rows: a restart loses every in-flight trip

slides.title: Persist trips in a database
script: The first thing we need is a **database**, because a trip in progress, and certainly a payment, must survive a server restart. A relational database like PostgreSQL is a natural first choice: we have **riders**, **drivers**, **trips** and **payments**, which reference each other, and we want transactions around changes like "assign this driver to this trip".

slides.title: The data model, naively
script: The trips table holds the pickup, dropoff, rider, driver, fare and, crucially, a **status** column. The naive move is to also put driver locations in the database: a *drivers* table with *lat* and *lng* columns, updated on every ping, and a "nearby drivers" query like *WHERE lat BETWEEN … AND lng BETWEEN …*.

slides.title: Failure one: write volume
script: This is the point where I'd stop and look at the numbers from the last slide, because this design fails in two specific ways. First, **write volume**. 1.25 million UPDATEs a second, each one durably written to a log and replicated, for data that's obsolete four seconds later. We'd be paying for durability on the least valuable data in the system.

items.detail: 5M drivers, one ping every 4 s
WAL write, fsync, ship to replicas
the next ping overwrites it

items.text: Durability spent on the **least valuable data**
items.detail: while trips and payments compete for the same disks

slides.title: Failure two: a 2-D query
script: Second, **the query**. A B-tree index on latitude, or even a composite index, handles a two-dimensional range badly: it narrows by latitude and then scans a long strip of the planet for longitude. Spatial index extensions help with the query but not the write rate.

rows: narrows by latitude, scans a strip of the planet
still a durable write per ping

slides.title: Trips and money only
script: So the database stays, but only for the data that deserves it, which is trips and money. Locations need a different home. First, though, let's pull those two kinds of traffic apart.

slides.title: Split by traffic shape: trips vs. locations
script: The single server is doing two jobs with completely different profiles, so let's split it. The **Trip Service** owns the business workflow: quotes, requests, cancellations, the trip's state. It handles the trickle, a couple of thousand requests per second, each of which matters. The **Location Service** takes the firehose of driver pings: high volume, tiny payloads, and individually almost worthless.

slides.title: Scale and fail independently
script: Splitting lets them **scale and fail independently**. The location tier can be a big fleet of simple ingest nodes. If it falls behind, positions get a little stale but trips keep working. A bug in trip logic doesn't stop us from knowing where cars are. They also deploy at different speeds: pricing and trip rules change constantly, while location ingest barely changes.

rows: a big fleet of simple ingest nodes
positions go a little stale; trips keep working

slides.title: An API gateway in front
script: Riders' requests now go through an **API gateway**, which handles TLS, authentication, rate limiting and routing to the right service, so individual services don't each reimplement that. Driver pings go straight to the location service for now. We'll give drivers a better channel shortly.

slides.title: Cleaning up every ping
script: The Location Service also does a little real work on each ping: it **validates** it (drop impossible jumps, bad accuracy) and **map-matches** it, snapping a noisy GPS point onto the road the car is actually on. A raw GPS fix in a city canyon can be off by 50 meters, which puts a driver on the wrong side of a river. It still writes to the database, which is the part we fix next.

bullets.heading: What the Location Service does with each ping

items.detail: drop impossible jumps and fixes with bad accuracy
snap the point onto the road the car is on (GPS can be 50 m off)
still to the database, for now (fixed next)

slides.title: The geo index: drivers bucketed into hexagonal cells
script: Locations move into a purpose-built **in-memory geo index**. The trick behind every geo index is the same: **turn two-dimensional positions into one-dimensional keys** so that "near me" becomes a handful of key lookups rather than a scan.

slides.title: Three ways to index space
script: There are three common options. A **geohash** interleaves the bits of latitude and longitude into a string, so nearby points tend to share a prefix. It's simple and works in any key-value store, but cells are rectangles that distort with latitude, and two points across a cell boundary can have very different prefixes. A **quadtree** splits space adaptively, subdividing busy areas like Manhattan more finely than empty desert, but it's a tree to keep balanced in memory as drivers move.

rows: interleaved lat/lng bits; neighbors share a prefix
a tree to rebalance as drivers move
a library to adopt (Uber open-sourced it)

slides.title: Why hexagons
script: Uber built and open-sourced **H3**, a grid of **hexagons** at multiple resolutions. Hexagons have a lovely property: all six neighbors are the same distance from the center, so "every cell within k steps" (a **k-ring**) approximates a circle well.
I'll use H3 at a resolution where a cell is a few hundred meters across.

items.detail: unlike a square's 4 edge and 4 corner neighbors
"every cell within k steps of the pickup"
we pick cells a few hundred meters across

slides.title: Inside the geo index
script: The index is just a map from **cell ID → set of driver IDs**, plus **driver ID → latest position and cell**. Each ping is an upsert: if the driver crossed into a new cell, move them between sets. Entries carry a **TTL** of around 30 seconds, so a driver whose phone died quietly disappears from the map instead of getting offers forever.

slides.title: Sharded by region, not durable
script: Half a gigabyte for the whole world fits on one machine, but the write rate doesn't, so we **shard by region**: each city's cells live on a small group of nodes, replicated for availability but **not durable**. If we lose a node, the next round of pings rebuilds it within seconds. That's the trade-off that makes 1.25 million writes a second cheap.

items.detail: fits on one machine; 1.25M writes/s doesn't
each city's cells on a small group of nodes
no disk log on the write path

items.text: **Lose a node?** The next pings rebuild it
items.detail: within seconds, because every driver pings every 4 s

slides.title: A dispatch service owns matching
script: Matching gets its own service: **Dispatch**. When the Trip Service creates a ride request, it asks Dispatch to find a driver. Dispatch queries the geo index for drivers near the pickup and decides who gets the offer.

slides.title: System of record vs. decision engine
script: Why separate this from the Trip Service? Because matching is where the interesting, fast-changing logic lives, and it has a different consistency shape from the trip itself. The Trip Service is the **system of record** for a trip: it's careful, transactional, and tells you what happened. Dispatch is a **real-time decision engine**: it keeps hot in-memory state about which drivers are free, which have outstanding offers, and how demand is building up in each area, and it makes thousands of decisions a second. Its algorithms get tuned constantly (Uber has been through many generations of matching), and isolating them keeps that churn away from the trip record.

rows: hot, in memory: free drivers, open offers, demand

slides.title: Partitioned by geography
script: Dispatch is also naturally **partitioned by geography**. A pickup in Chicago only ever competes for drivers in Chicago. So we shard dispatch by region, with each instance owning a set of H3 cells.

items.detail: a Chicago pickup only competes for Chicago drivers
no cross-city coordination on the hot path

items.text: Each instance **owns a set of H3 cells**
items.detail: its drivers, its offers, its demand

slides.title: One owner per area
script: Uber's own dispatch system used a consistent-hashing ring to assign ownership, so any node can forward a request to the node that owns that area. Having **one owner per area** also makes the hardest invariant much easier, as we'll see: two requests that could both want the same driver are handled by the same process.

steps.label: find a driver near cell X

steps.note: all requests near cell X land on node 3

slides.title: Maps and ETAs: distance is the wrong metric
script: There's a problem with "closest driver". **Straight-line distance is a poor proxy for how long a driver will take to arrive.** A driver 300 meters away on the other side of a river, a highway or a one-way grid might be 10 minutes out, while one a kilometer away on the same road is three minutes out. What the rider experiences, and what wastes drivers' time, is **ETA**.

slides.title: Inside the Maps / ETA service
script: So Dispatch calls a **Maps / ETA service**. I said in the requirements that I'm not designing this, so it's drawn as a dashed box. But it's worth saying what it does: it holds a road graph with turn restrictions and **live traffic speeds** (derived, conveniently, from our own drivers' location stream), runs a fast routing algorithm (contraction hierarchies or similar, so a route is milliseconds rather than a full Dijkstra over a continent), and corrects the result with an ML model trained on actual past trip times.

bullets.heading: What the Maps / ETA service does (not designed here)

items.detail: one-way streets, rivers, highway exits
derived from our own drivers' location stream
contraction hierarchies: milliseconds, not a continent-wide Dijkstra
trained on actual past trip times

slides.title: One call, many ETAs
script: The interface we need is **many-to-one**: "here are 30 candidate drivers; give me each one's ETA to this pickup" in a single call. Doing 30 separate routing requests would blow the latency budget.

slides.title: Who uses ETAs, and the fallback
script: The same service will be used again later by pricing (the route and expected duration determine the fare) and by the rider app to show "your driver is 4 minutes away". Because it's on the critical path for matching, Dispatch should **degrade gracefully** if it's slow: fall back to distance multiplied by a typical city speed, rather than failing the match.
Dispatch is now the heart of the system, so let's zoom in on it.

rows: critical path: if slow, distance × city speed

slides.title: Matching deep dive ①: candidate search
script: We're now inside the Dispatch Service, following a single ride request, trip T42, from left to right. The goal of this pipeline: **pick one driver, quickly, without ever double-booking**, and do it in a way that's good for the whole city and not just this one rider.

slides.title: Expanding rings
script: Step one is **candidate search**. We convert the pickup point into its H3 cell and ask the geo index for the drivers in that cell and its first ring of neighbors. If that returns too few drivers, say fewer than 10 or 20, we **expand** to the next ring, and the next, up to a cap of a few kilometers. In dense downtown areas the first ring is plenty. In the suburbs we might go out several rings.

steps.note: downtown: ring 1 is plenty · suburbs: several rings, capped at a few km

slides.title: Key lookups, and over-fetch
script: Two details matter here. The search is a set of **direct key lookups**, one per cell, rather than a range scan, so it's fast and its cost is predictable. And we deliberately **over-fetch**: we want a pool of perhaps 20–50 drivers, not just the nearest one, because the next steps will discard some and reorder the rest.

items.detail: no range scan: fast, with a predictable cost
the next steps discard some and reorder the rest

slides.title: Plausible, not final
script: Positions in the index are a few seconds stale, which is fine at this stage. We're finding *plausible* candidates, not making a final decision. Accuracy matters later, when we compute ETAs from each driver's most recent ping.

rows: a few seconds stale is fine

slides.title: Matching deep dive ②: filter on driver state
script: Next we **filter** the candidate pool. Being near the pickup isn't enough; a driver must actually be eligible.

slides.title: The driver state machine
script: The most important check is **driver state**. Dispatch keeps a small state machine per driver: **offline**, **free**, **offered** (an offer is outstanding and we're waiting for an answer), and **on trip**. Only free drivers pass, with one useful exception: a driver who's on trip but **about to drop off** nearby can be considered for a back-to-back trip. That keeps busy drivers busy, and it's often faster for the rider than someone further away who's idle.

rows: only if about to drop off nearby (back-to-back)

slides.title: Product rules
script: Then the product rules: the right **vehicle type** (UberX vs. XL vs. Black), wheelchair-accessible if requested, airport queue rules, and any **preferences or blocks** such as a rider and driver who rated each other one star and should not be paired again.

items.detail: UberX vs. XL vs. Black
if requested
a one-star pair is never matched again

slides.title: Where driver state lives
script: Where does driver state live? It's owned by Dispatch, in memory, in the same regional shard as the geo index for that area, so this filter costs no network hops. It's **more important than location**, so it is replicated and changes to it are logged, but it's still kept separate from the trip record.

slides.title: Assigned vs. busy
script: The trip record says "trip T42 was assigned driver D7". Driver state says "D7 is busy right now". We'll use this state to enforce exclusivity in a moment.

slides.title: Matching deep dive ③: rank by ETA
script: Now we **rank** the eligible drivers, and as I argued earlier, the primary signal is **ETA to the pickup**, not distance. We send the whole filtered set to the Maps service as one many-to-one request and get back an ETA matrix.

slides.title: More than ETA
script: ETA alone isn't the whole score, though. A real ranking might also weigh things like **heading** (a driver pointed toward the pickup beats one facing away, even at equal ETA, since U-turns are slow and error-prone), the driver's **acceptance likelihood** (a driver who declines most offers wastes the rider's time), and **fairness**, spreading trips across drivers who've been waiting a long time rather than always picking the same lucky one parked downtown.

rows: the primary signal: what the rider experiences
facing the pickup beats facing away; U-turns are slow
a driver who declines most offers wastes the rider's time
favor drivers who've waited long, not the lucky one downtown

slides.title: A tunable scoring function
script: I'd keep this as a scoring function: weighted terms whose weights get tuned with experiments, because the "right" balance between rider wait time and driver utilization is a business decision, not an engineering one.

items.detail: one per signal
A/B tests per city
a business decision, not an engineering one

slides.title: Ranked candidates for T42
script: The output of this stage is an ordered list of drivers for trip T42. The obvious next step would be "offer the trip to the top driver". But that's **greedy**, and greedy matching has a problem.

slides.title: Matching deep dive ④: batch matching beats greedy
script: Picture two riders, A and B, requesting a second apart, and two free drivers, 1 and 2. Driver 1 is 2 minutes from A and 3 minutes from B. Driver 2 is 10 minutes from A but 4 minutes from B.

slides.title: Greedy depends on arrival order
script: Greedy, first-come-first-served matching gives A driver 1 (2 minutes), and B is left with driver 2 (4 minutes): 6 minutes of total waiting. That happens to be fine. But reverse the arrival order and greedy gives B driver 1 (3 minutes) and A driver 2 (10 minutes): 13 minutes total, when 6 was available. **The order requests arrive in shouldn't decide the outcome.**

slides.title: Collect, then solve
script: So instead of matching each request the instant it arrives, Dispatch **collects requests in a short window**, on the order of a couple of seconds, for each area. It then solves a **global assignment** over every open request and free driver in that area together. That's a classic bipartite matching problem: minimize total ETA, with the same fairness and acceptance terms as cost adjustments. The Hungarian algorithm or a min-cost-flow solver handles a few hundred by a few hundred in milliseconds.

slides.title: Two seconds for shorter pickups
script: The trade-off is explicit: we **add up to ~2 seconds of latency** to every match in exchange for **shorter average pickups and higher driver utilization** across the city. Riders don't notice 2 seconds against a 4-minute pickup; they very much notice a 10-minute one. In quiet areas with only a single request in the window, this simply reduces to greedy. And because each dispatch shard owns its area, the optimizer sees every competing request there, with no cross-node coordination needed.

items.text: **Cost:** up to ~2 s more per match
items.detail: unnoticeable against a 4-minute pickup
riders do notice a 10-minute pickup
one request in the window
each shard owns its area and sees every competing request

slides.title: Matching deep dive ⑤: the offer and the driver lock
script: Finally, the **Offer Manager** turns an assignment into an actual match, and this is where we enforce the core invariant: **a driver is never assigned to two trips**.
Before sending an offer, it **locks** the driver by atomically moving their state from *free* to *offered(T42)*.

slides.title: Compare-and-set with a TTL
script: That's a **compare-and-set**: it succeeds only if the driver is still free. If anything else got there first, the CAS fails and we take the next driver. The lock has a **TTL** of about 15 seconds, the offer timeout. So if Dispatch crashes mid-offer, or the driver's phone vanishes, the driver frees up automatically rather than being stuck forever.

steps.label: CAS D7: free → offered(T42), TTL 15 s

steps.note: Dispatch crashes or the phone vanishes: after 15 s, D7 → free

slides.title: Exactly one place the lock lives
script: Because one dispatch shard owns the area, this CAS is local and fast. For drivers near a shard boundary, ownership of the *driver* follows their current cell, so there's still exactly one place the lock lives.

items.detail: the shard that owns the area holds the driver's state
the driver is owned by the shard of their current cell
no distributed lock needed

slides.title: Accept, decline or time out
script: Then the offer goes to the **driver's app**. Three outcomes: **accept**, and Dispatch tells the Trip Service, which records driver D7 on trip T42 and moves it to **MATCHED**; **decline**; or **timeout**. On either of the last two we release the lock and loop back to the optimizer for the **next best** driver, typically excluding this one for this trip.

slides.title: One driver at a time
script: Why offer to **one driver at a time** rather than broadcasting to five and taking the first to tap? Broadcasting is faster, but four drivers get a notification that disappears in their hands, which trains them to ignore offers and feels terrible. Sequential offers with a short timeout are the better product. Some systems compromise by offering to a second driver if the first hasn't responded within a few seconds.

rows: four offers vanish in drivers' hands
a second driver after a few seconds

slides.title: That's matching
script: That's matching. Let's zoom back out and fix how all these messages actually reach the phones.

slides.title: A realtime gateway: persistent connections for drivers
script: Back in the full system. The offer manager needs to reach a specific driver's phone **within a second**, and so far drivers only poll. Polling every second would cost battery and multiply our request rate; polling every 10 seconds would eat most of the 15-second offer window. So drivers keep a **persistent connection** to a new **Realtime Gateway** tier, a WebSocket or a similar long-lived stream.

slides.title: One connection, both directions
script: That connection is two-way, so it carries traffic in both directions. Location pings go **up** it, which is much cheaper than a fresh HTTPS request every 4 seconds: no repeated handshakes or headers, just a few bytes per message. Offers come **down** it, and the driver's accept or decline goes back up.

slides.title: Thin, stateful gateways
script: The gateways are **stateful**: each one holds hundreds of thousands of open connections, so we keep them deliberately thin. They authenticate the connection, keep a registry of **which gateway holds which driver**, and forward messages; all decisions stay in the services behind them. When Dispatch wants to offer trip T42 to driver D7, it looks up D7's gateway and sends the message there.

slides.title: Surviving disconnects
script: Mobile connections are flaky, so the protocol has to assume **disconnects**. Every downstream message has a sequence number, and the app acknowledges what it has received. On reconnect, to any gateway, the app says "I last saw message 812" and the gateway replays anything newer. An offer that's already expired is simply not replayed.

steps.note: tunnel: the connection drops; 813 and 814 are queued
an expired offer is not replayed

slides.title: Live tracking for riders
script: Riders need the same channel. Once a trip is matched, the rider app opens a connection to the Realtime Gateway and **subscribes** to that trip. Two kinds of message flow to it.

slides.title: What a rider's connection carries
script: The **Trip Service** pushes status changes: "driver assigned", "arriving", "trip started". The **Location Service** forwards the assigned driver's position as each ping arrives, so the car moves smoothly on the rider's map.

slides.title: Tiny fan-out, smooth movement
script: The location fan-out here is **tiny**: one driver's pings go to one rider (or a handful of people sharing their trip status). It isn't like a chat channel with thousands of members. The Location Service keeps a small map of *driver → subscribers* for active trips and forwards each ping to the right gateway. The client also **interpolates** between pings along the route, so a 4-second update interval still looks like smooth movement.

items.detail: or a handful sharing the trip; not a chat channel with thousands
kept by the Location Service, for active trips only

items.text: Each ping goes to **the right gateway**
items.detail: the one holding each subscriber's connection
a 4-second interval still looks smooth

slides.title: Push as a fallback
script: What if the app isn't running? A driver who's online but has switched to another app, or whose OS has suspended the connection, can't receive an offer over a socket. So the gateway falls back to **APNs / FCM** push notifications to **wake the app**, which then reconnects and pulls the pending offer.

slides.title: Push is the doorbell
script: Push alone isn't reliable or fast enough to carry the offer itself, but it's a good doorbell. The same mechanism tells a rider "your driver has arrived" when their phone is in their pocket.

slides.title: The trip record and a sharded trip store
script: Now let's look harder at the **trip** itself, the record that must be exactly right.

slides.title: The trip state machine
script: A trip is a **state machine**: *REQUESTED → MATCHED → DRIVER_ARRIVING → IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED*, with *CANCELLED* reachable from most states. The Trip Service is the only writer, and only legal transitions are allowed.

slides.title: The race: cancel vs. accept
script: The danger is **races**. The rider taps cancel at the same moment the driver taps accept. Two Trip Service instances process them concurrently. If both just read the row, decide, and write, we end up with a cancelled trip that has a driver driving to it.

steps.note: a cancelled trip with a driver driving to it

slides.title: Conditional writes
script: The fix is **conditional writes**: every update says "set status = MATCHED *where status = REQUESTED and version = 7*". Exactly one of the racing writes wins, and the loser re-reads and reacts, telling the driver "sorry, the rider cancelled". Every transition also carries an **idempotency key** from the client, so a retried "start trip" tap is harmless.

slides.title: Sharded by city
script: The single PostgreSQL primary becomes a **sharded Trip Store**, partitioned by **city** (or region) and then by trip ID. City sharding matches how everything else is partitioned, keeps a city's hot data together, and lets one region's database fail without touching others.

bullets.heading: Partition by city, then by trip ID

items.detail: geo index, dispatch and gateways are already per region
one region's database fails without touching others

slides.title: Choosing the trip store
script: I'd use a store with strongly consistent single-row conditional writes: sharded MySQL or Postgres, or a NewSQL store like Spanner or CockroachDB. Uber built its own, Schemaless and later Docstore, on top of MySQL. At a couple of thousand trips per second the volume is modest; the hard requirement is correctness.
Completed trips are rarely updated, so after some months they can move to cheaper storage for history and receipts.

table.heading: Must have: strongly consistent single-row conditional writes
rows: NewSQL: sharding and replication built in
what Uber built, on top of MySQL

slides.title: An event log: Kafka for trip and location events
script: A lot of things want to **react** to what's happening on the platform: pricing wants to know where demand and supply are; payments need to know a trip completed; analytics, fraud and ETA-model training want everything. We don't want the Trip Service calling each of those synchronously. It would be slow, fragile, and every new consumer would mean a change to the core service.
So we add **Kafka** as the platform's event log.

slides.title: Two topics, keyed for order
script: The Trip Service publishes an event for every state transition: *trip_requested*, *trip_matched*, *trip_completed*, and so on. The Location Service publishes the location stream, possibly sampled down for consumers that don't need every ping. Topics are partitioned by trip ID or driver ID, so events about the same entity stay in order.

slides.title: When the write and the event disagree
script: One subtlety: the trip write and the event publish must not **disagree**. If we commit the trip and then crash before publishing, payments would never hear the trip ended.

steps.note: payments never hears that T42 ended

slides.title: The transactional outbox
script: The standard fix is a **transactional outbox**: write the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the trip update, and have a relay publish the outbox to Kafka. Alternatively, use change-data-capture on the trip store. Either way, consumers see every event **at least once**, so each consumer must be idempotent.

steps.label: one txn: T42 COMPLETED + outbox row

slides.title: Replay
script: Kafka also gives us **replay**. A new consumer, or a fixed buggy one, can rewind and reprocess history. The next few slides are all consumers of this log.

items.text: A **new consumer** rewinds and reads history
items.detail: no backfill job against the trip store
from the offset before the bug
surge, payments, the data lake

slides.title: Pricing: upfront fare quotes
script: Back to the very first thing the rider sees: an **upfront fare**. When the rider sets a destination, the app asks the **Pricing Service** for a quote, via the gateway, for each product (UberX, XL, Comfort and so on).

slides.title: Building the fare
script: The base fare comes from the **route**: Pricing asks the Maps service for the expected distance and duration from pickup to dropoff, then applies the city's rate card (base fee + per-minute + per-kilometer + booking fee, with minimums, tolls and airport surcharges). Then it multiplies by the current **surge multiplier** for the pickup area, which we'll compute on the next slide.

slides.title: A quote is a commitment
script: The important design point is that the quote is a **commitment**. Pricing returns a **quote ID** with the price and an expiry, a few minutes, and stores it, or signs it so it can't be tampered with. When the rider hits request, the Trip Service checks that the quote is still valid and locks that price into the trip.

slides.title: What the quote guarantees
script: That way the rider pays what they were shown, even if the surge changes in the seconds between the quote and the tap. It also means an expensive quote isn't silently re-priced. If the quote expired, the app asks for a new one and shows it.

rows: the rider pays the quoted price
the app asks for a new one and shows it

slides.title: A read-heavy path
script: Quotes are a **read-heavy** path: people check prices far more often than they request. Pricing is stateless and scales horizontally, and the surge multiplier it reads is a precomputed value, not something computed per request.

items.detail: people compare products and times before booking
scales horizontally behind the gateway
a lookup, not a computation per request

slides.title: Surge: streaming supply and demand per hex cell
script: Surge pricing exists to **rebalance the market**. When demand in an area outstrips the drivers available, a higher price both tempers demand and pulls drivers toward that area. To do that we need a live picture of supply and demand per area, and Kafka already carries both.

slides.title: Counting supply and demand
script: A **stream processor** (Flink, say) consumes the event log and, for each H3 cell, maintains **sliding-window counts** over the last few minutes: **demand** from *trip_requested* events (plus app opens, since people who check a price and leave are demand too), and **supply** from free drivers in the location stream.

steps.label: app opened in cell c → demand +1
free driver ping in cell c → supply
sliding window: last few minutes, per cell

slides.title: From counts to a multiplier
script: Every minute or so it computes a multiplier from the ratio, **smoothed** across neighboring cells and over time, so prices don't jump wildly or flicker block by block. The result is written to a small **Surge Store** (a key-value store keyed by cell) that the Pricing Service reads on every quote.

slides.title: A minute behind, on purpose
script: A few deliberate choices here. Surge is **eventually consistent** and a minute or so behind reality. That's fine, and it's actually desirable: a multiplier that changed every second would be impossible for a driver to act on.

items.detail: a minute or so behind reality
a multiplier that changed every second is impossible to act on

slides.title: Off the critical path, capped by policy
script: It's **off the critical path**: if the pipeline stalls, Pricing uses the last value and then falls back to 1.0× after it goes stale, so a pipeline failure costs revenue, not rides. And it's per city, with **caps** set by policy. Some cities and emergencies legally limit surge, so the cap is a business rule applied at quote time, not hard-coded in the pipeline.

rows: falls back to 1.0×: lost revenue, not lost rides
clamps the multiplier at quote time (a business rule)

slides.title: Payments: exactly-once charges
script: When a trip reaches **COMPLETED**, the rider must be charged **exactly once**. The **Payment Service** consumes *trip_completed* from Kafka. It's asynchronous on purpose: the rider shouldn't wait on a card network to get out of the car, and if the processor is down we want to retry later, not fail the trip.

slides.title: Idempotency is the core
script: "At least once" delivery from Kafka plus retries everywhere is a recipe for double charges, so **idempotency** is the core of this service. Every charge has an **idempotency key** derived from the trip, like *charge:T42*.

items.detail: the same trip_completed can arrive twice
after timeouts, crashes, deploys
derived from the trip: charge:T42

slides.title: A retry finds the existing charge
script: The Payment Service records the payment intent under that key before calling out, and passes the same key to the **payment processor** (Stripe, Braintree, Adyen), which also deduplicates on it. A redelivered event or a retry after a timeout finds the existing record and either returns its result or resumes it. It never creates a second charge.

slides.title: Pre-authorize at request time
script: Many teams also **pre-authorize** the card for the quoted amount at request time, so the charge at the end rarely fails.

slides.title: A double-entry ledger
script: Money is tracked in a **double-entry ledger**: an append-only log where every movement is a balanced pair of entries.

slides.title: Balanced, append-only entries
script: The rider's card is debited for the fare; the driver's earnings account, Uber's fee and taxes are credited. Entries are never updated or deleted. A refund is a new, reversing entry.

slides.title: Reconciliation and payouts
script: That makes the books auditable and lets a daily **reconciliation** job compare our ledger against the processor's settlement reports and flag any mismatch. Driver payouts are then a periodic batch job over their earnings balance.

items.detail: every movement is an entry; nothing is rewritten
our ledger vs. the processor's settlement reports; flag mismatches
a periodic batch over each driver's earnings balance

slides.title: The data lake: analytics and the models that feed back in
script: Every event on Kafka also lands in a **data lake**: columnar files on object storage (Parquet on S3 or HDFS), queried with Spark, Presto or Hive. Trips, location traces, offers and whether they were accepted, quotes and whether they converted. This is where the offline side of the business lives.

slides.title: Analytics, and a feedback loop
script: Some of it is classic analytics: city operations dashboards, finance, experiment analysis. But a lot of it **feeds back into the online system**, and that's why it's on the architecture diagram.

items.detail: city operations dashboards, finance, experiment analysis
models and parameters the live services use

slides.title: What feeds back online
script: The **ETA model** that corrects the routing engine is trained on billions of real trips: predicted vs. actual arrival times. The **acceptance-likelihood** scores used in dispatch ranking come from historical offer outcomes. **Surge** parameters and the matching optimizer's weights are tuned by replaying past demand in simulation. Supply positioning, nudging idle drivers toward where demand will be in 15 minutes, comes from demand forecasts trained here.

rows: billions of trips: predicted vs. actual arrival
where demand will be in 15 minutes

slides.title: Ratings and trip history
script: Ratings and trip history fit here too. A rating is just a small write through the Trip Service at the end of a trip. A driver's average rating is an aggregate that's recomputed in batch and pushed back to the profile, rather than computed live. The trip history list in the app reads from the trip store, and older trips fall back to archived storage.

rows: a small write through the Trip Service
aggregated in the lake, like every event
pushed back to the driver's profile
recent from the trip store; older from the archive

slides.title: Nothing online depends on the lake
script: The key principle: **nothing online depends on the lake being up**. Models and parameters are published back to the online services as artifacts, so the lake can be slow or down without affecting a single ride.

steps.note: lake down: online keeps serving v42

slides.title: Going global: regions and cells
script: Finally, **going global**. Ride-hailing is the most partitionable system I can think of: a trip starts and ends in one city. So the natural unit of deployment is a **cell**: a full copy of this stack serving a set of cities, in a nearby region.

slides.title: Cells limit the blast radius
script: Requests are routed to the cell that owns the city at the rider's location. A bad deploy or a database problem then affects a few cities, not the planet, and we roll out changes cell by cell.

items.detail: to the cell that owns the city at the rider's location
a bad deploy or a database problem hits a few cities, not the planet
watch one cell before the next

slides.title: The hard part: trips in flight
script: Each cell's trip store is **replicated to a standby region**. If a region fails, its cities fail over. The hard part is the trips already in flight. Replication is asynchronous (synchronous cross-region writes would add latency to every transition), so the standby may be a few seconds behind.

steps.note: region A fails before T42's update reaches B
the standby still thinks T42 is MATCHED

slides.title: The driver's phone as a replica
script: Uber's answer is neat: the **driver's phone** holds a signed, encrypted copy of the current trip state, updated on each transition. After failover, when the driver app reconnects to the new region, it hands that state back, and the backend restores any trips it missed. The phone acts as a last-resort replica that's always in the right place.

steps.note: region A fails · its cities fail over to B

slides.title: The rest rebuilds itself
script: The rest rebuilds itself. The **geo index** isn't replicated at all: within seconds of failover, drivers' pings repopulate it from scratch. **Dispatch** state (who's free, who has an offer) is rebuilt from the trip store plus fresh pings. Surge falls back to defaults until the pipeline catches up. Money flows stay exactly-once because of the idempotency keys, even if a charge is retried from the other region.

table.heading: After a regional failover
rows: not replicated: drivers' pings repopulate it in seconds

slides.title: The complete system: following one ride end to end
script: To close, let me follow one ride through the finished system. Maya, in Chicago, opens the app at 11pm outside a concert.

Her app asks the **Pricing Service** for a quote through the **API gateway**. Pricing gets the route from **Maps** and the multiplier for her H3 cell from the **Surge Store**, where the **surge pipeline** has already noticed requests spiking and free drivers thinning out. She sees $24, valid for two minutes, and taps request. The **Trip Service** validates the quote and writes trip T42 as REQUESTED to the **Trip Store**, emitting an event to **Kafka**.

**Dispatch** takes it. It pulls candidates from the **geo index** (fed by 1.25 million pings a second through the **Realtime Gateways** and **Location Service**), filters to free drivers, ranks them by real ETA, and solves a two-second batch together with the 40 other requests outside the venue. It locks driver D7 with a compare-and-set and offers the trip down D7's WebSocket. D7 accepts; the Trip Service moves T42 to MATCHED with a conditional write. Maya watches D7's car approach in real time. Twenty minutes later the trip is COMPLETED, and the **Payment Service** charges her card exactly once using the key *charge:T42*, writing balanced entries to the **ledger**. All of it lands in the **data lake**, and next week's ETA model is a little better for it.

The themes I'd underline: **separate the firehose from the trickle**, with locations in memory and lossy while trips are durable and strongly consistent; **geography is the partition key** for the geo index, dispatch, storage and failover alike; **one owner per area** plus a compare-and-set lock, so a driver is never double-booked; **batch matching on ETA** rather than greedy matching on distance; and an **event log** so pricing, payments and analytics react without slowing the ride down. With more time I'd go deeper on shared rides (Pool turns matching into a routing problem), on fraud, and on how the ETA model itself is built.
